utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom and while doing so, I'd like to first inform the parties that, unfortunately, we cannot sit on Thursday in the morning, so we have to stick to the schedule, although everyone would have preferred to sit in the morning. The second issue is that rumours told me that there would be a letter on its way. It's even -- or said that it was a seven-page letter, dated already last week. We haven't received it. So if there's a letter on its way and if someone sent it to us, then a courtesy copy might speed up the Judges dealing with the letter. So it's just for whomever did write us a letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think this is -- well, I think I can solve this particular mystery quite quickly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wrote such a letter, so I assume that is what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I sent it very specifically and directly addressed to Trial Chamber I, and I addressed it to Your Honours. So I naturally expected it would find its way to you. But this is a very large building. I understand that. But of course, Your Honour, we can easily produce a copy of that letter during the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not saying -- since I do not know, although rumours tell me something about it as well, but we can't even start thinking about it if we haven't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, of course I entirely understand that. It is -- I may just comment. It is a little bit extraordinary that the rumours can pass in the building but a simple piece of paper can't find its way across a corridor. But that's another matter. Your Honour, we will produce a copy of that letter if that's from a practical point of view helpful. Because clearly until Your Honours receive something there's not much you can do with it, is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You know rumours always go quicker than anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I remind you as usual that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and I'll now give an opportunity to Mr. Stewart to proceed with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I say, if Your Honours need any guidance at any point as to the physical matter of which files to bring into court for which sessions, then I'll be happy to help, but I think at the moment Your Honours probably have something up to about 5 or 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got 4 to 6 with me, and also the transcripts and the intercepts. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There shouldn't be any problem until the first break, Your Honour, in that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, good morning.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder if we could take, then, file or bundle 3. And this relates to the Political Council of the SDS, 15th of October, 1991. And you particularly drew attention to items on the second page. I'm talking always in my case of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Tab 47. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's where we ended yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 47, second page. And in the middle of the page you drew attention to Mr. Krajisnik. We should not start from the standpoint that the coalition has adopted a decision, because they have not adopted in a legal manner. And of course when he refers to coalition, he's referring to the SDA and the HDZ, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And secondly, since the above-mentioned decision is illegal and unconstitutional, we must find a method of proving this. So it's apparent, isn't it, at this stage, Mr. Treanor, that Mr. Krajisnik is wishing, on the basis of what he says here, to proceed through legal mechanisms to try to resolve this stand-off between the SDS and the other parties?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if I get that out of this passage. The reason why I thought it was important was because it indicated the view of the SDS leadership in general and Mr. Krajisnik in particular, of the nature of the action that had been taken by the coalition partners what their appraisal of that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It goes a bit further than that, doesn't it. Of course, we know that the SDS did not accept the legality and constitutionality of the position taken by the other parties. We know that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And that was a consistent position, wasn't it? It's not just here, but that was their consistent position.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Mr. Krajisnik is talking about finding a method of proving this. And then if we go on, then Mrs. Plavsic talks about asking for a slot on television for the president of the Assembly to address the public and explain what happened. And then at the end of that passage: The entire procedure should be forwarded for verification to the expert legal commission. And then of course lots of other people are coming in saying that it was illegal, unconstitutional. Mr. Neskovic takes a different view. But the -- but can't we get a bit more than your indicating from this, Mr. Treanor, that they're wanting to explain to the public the -- what they see as the illegality, they're wanting to get some backing and verification of their views on the illegality and try to deal with the matter by demonstrating that what's been done hasn't been legitimately done?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what they're discussing, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, if we go on, please, to tab 49. And then you drew attention to the second paragraph on page 3. Well, in fact, it's the second full paragraph, is what I'm talking about, starting from this organisation of the MUP, it says Ministry of the Interior. And just to remind ourselves, this is a document setting out the possibility of organising a Serbian Ministry of the Interior. So this is 17th of October. This is just a few days after that particular crisis in the Assembly. And this is -- I'm sorry, to give the reference, it's 1431 of the transcript of your evidence. The existing -- starting with this organisation, that is the existing organisation of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, it's possible to establish a Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs as a parallel organ of authority. And it goes on to enumerate those ways. So item 1, going back to the document itself, paragraph 3. The possible ways of establishing are as follows: That the existing Ministry of the Interior should not be split, that the Serbian Assembly and the Serbian government should appoint a Serbian Ministry of the Interior and then install Serbian personnel in key positions. So the second sentence, or the last sentence in that paragraph: The Serbian MUP set up in this way would continue to function in cooperation with the existing MUP, with which it would be in contact regarding issues of common interest. Then of course item 2 goes on to an alternative possibility, which is to move the Serbian MUP out of the existing MUP. But it's -- Mr. Treanor, we do see, don't we here, would you agree, we do see considerable flexibility in the approach of the SDS at this point? And looking for ways of resolving the matter without a head-on split or conflict?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, indeed in this document discussing possibilities for establishing a Serbian MUP, various alternatives are considered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the first alternative, that the existing MUP should not be split, would in the context of what had happened at that time, and particularly the crisis which had occurred in the previous few days, would have been a very constructive way of approaching the matter, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that would depend on your point of view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you're the witness and the expert, and it's your point of view which is being sought, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I'm here to say what's constructive and so forth. I'm here to say what the documents -- indicate what the documents say and try to put them into some sort of context. I notice the date on this document. It's always good thing to look at the date of documents and consider what the situation was at that particular time, is the 17th of October, and reference is made here to a Serbian Assembly and a Serbian government, which didn't even exist yet. So I would say that some of the things they're considering here are -- would not have been considered constructive by other parties in Bosnia certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take possibility number 1, then, that the existing MUP organisation should not be split. Are you saying that -- if you say that other parties and that presumably is very simple code, let's say especially for the SDA, other parties might not have considered it to be constructive, what less than this could the SDA have reasonably expected the SDS to do as a reaction to what had happened in relation to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me to speculate now on what the SDA would have thought the SDS should have done?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What less could the SDS have done in the circumstances in relation to the future structure and organisation of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one thing that they could have done is nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Logically, that's right. Nothing would have been -- well, it would have been politically a very difficult position for the SDS to have adopted and it would have been rather an unrealistically lame response, wouldn't it, to the situation that they were faced with?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether it was unrealistic or lame or not, I don't know. You asked me what they could have done. That's one thing they could have done. What they are discussing doing in this paper is of course in one way or another splitting the ministry and establishing a Serbian ministry. That is in fact the response that they seem to be advocating here, whether this is one that the SDA would have thought that was reasonable, I could only speculate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, speculate. I want to perhaps try and see if we can see what the ground rules are here, if you like. A few minutes ago, when I asked you for a view, I think you said something like you were only here to say what the documents said. If you -- if you are only here, Mr. Treanor, to tell us what the documents say, then - and I don't mean this at all rudely - you could have saved yourself and everybody else a great deal of time, because the documents say what the documents say. I had understood, certainly from a lot of your evidence in chief, that, like many expert witnesses, you are also here to express views on matters connected with this case and arising out of the document within the limits of what you can properly know and say. Am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think what I said was I'm here to indicate what the documents say and help to put them into context for the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it may be, Mr. Treanor, that there's a difficult line sometimes between putting them into context and expressing views, but when I ask you to express a view, if you simply can't, if the answer is: Well, I just -- I, Mr. Treanor, just don't know enough about this or I wasn't there or we can't tell from the documents, that's a reasonable response. But if in putting the documents into a context you can offer a view, that would be helpful. Just going back to this document we've got in front of us, the -- you have indicated, if you like, a prior possibility. You've got numbers 1 and 2. Number 1 is that the existing -- on the document, number 1 is that the existing organisation should not be split. Number 2 is that it should be split. You put before that logically the possibility that they could do absolutely nothing at all, and simply allow the MUP to continue in its present form. And I'm suggesting to you that that prior possibility that they should just do nothing was completely unrealistic for the SDS, given that what they were faced with and the decisions and declarations made by the other parties, that that was the context.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's apparent that they certainly considered a null option to be unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you know a lot about the context, and with your clearly more objective view than the view of the members of the SDS who were there at the time, from your objective viewpoint, wouldn't it have been an absolutely politically unrealistic position for the SDS to adopt, to say: Well, let's do nothing. We're faced with this situation. Let's just let the MUP carry on as it is.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure whether I'm going to be speculating or not, but you seem to be interested in this issue, in the Serbian view, the view of the SDS leadership of the situation in MUP and what could be done about it. As some of the documents indicated from an earlier period going back to the summer of 1991, the SDS leadership was unhappy with the situation in MUP, in particular, the personnel situation. They were, among other things, unhappy with the performance of some of their own designees in the ministry, in particular Mr. Zepinic, who they felt had become -- seemed to have felt had become a tool of the minister, Mr. Delimustafic. One possibility that they might have explored would have been replacing Mr. Zepinic with someone more forceful and reliable, in order to force the type of personnel policy which they wished to see in the ministry. That is one possible line of action within the framework of their concerns as I see them, and I think I could sit here and speculate all day as to different things that they could have done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on, then, if we may, to same bundle but tab 50. These are minutes of a session of the Deputies' Club of the SDS on the 18th of October, 1991. And you dealt with this at page 1441, the transcript of your evidence. And you particularly looked at page 4. You drew the -- there were other items, of course, to which you drew the Court's attention, but Dr. Karadzic's comments, page 4 of the English translation, point 29. You said: A team -- you -- well, Dr. Karadzic said. Do you see that? The team made up of the leading men of the party, the government, and the Political Council has been working day and night. I have decided to impose a state of emergency on the party. Please inform the others -- inform others that the party is working in emergency conditions. We must not take a single wrong step. Listen to our leaders. Maximum discipline is required. Mr. Treanor, do you have, from your inspection of the documents and your knowledge of the context, do you have any knowledge of who was in that team?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the specific reference to the team is an ad hoc reference. I don't know exactly who he had in mind at that particular point in time when he was speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you in fact know whether it was correct that there had been any such team working day and night?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it's apparent from the documentation which exists from this period, including the minutes of various meetings, telephone conversations, et cetera, that there was -- this was an intense period of interaction among the members of the leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Treanor, I think we can agree about that. There was lots happening. But from what you've seen on the documents, have you actually seen anything to indicate whether there was actually anything that could reasonably be identified as a team in the way that Dr. Karadzic was referring to it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, and there are some documents that were discussed in the course of my presentation relating to the establishment of -- I forget what the exact term was. I believe it was the -- something like the National Security Council of the SDS and the whole reporting structure that they had laid out. It could be that there was something like that in operation at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in particular, to be very specific --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm just trying to link that with the document. I realise it's slightly speculative, but I'm trying to find a documentary basis to respond to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you. Thank you, Mr. Treanor. I appreciate that, and we always have to see, don't we, where the limits of where you can go on what you know. The -- to be specific, do you, for example, have any idea whether Mr. Krajisnik was involved in any such team activity at that time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that Mr. Krajisnik was involved in these series of meetings and consultations that took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in fact, inevitably would pretty much always have been involved in discussions from his standpoint and his position as the president or the Speaker of the Assembly, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree that he would inevitably have been involved in these discussions. But that they would have been solely as a result of his position as Speaker of the Assembly, I don't know, because of course that was not the case. He was not solely the Speaker of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that he was, because we can see indisputable other positions that he had. There may be some in dispute, but we can see some positions are indisputable. But it is correct, is it, Mr. Treanor, that throughout this whole period, late October -- sorry, late 1991 and right into 1992, Mr. Krajisnik's duties and responsibilities as Speaker of the Assembly, and in a sense it doesn't matter which Assembly you're talking about, the BH Assembly before and then the Serb Assembly afterwards, would have taken a very great deal of his time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how much of his time it might have taken. The Speaker of the SR BiH Assembly had the duty of presiding at joint sessions of that Assembly, which were rather infrequent. The session at which the memorandum and the platform were adopted was the 8th joint session. The 9th joint session didn't take place until January. So it wouldn't appear that he was particularly busy being the president of the Assembly of SR BH from that point of view. The setting up of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, which he was elected president, was -- is a matter that I presume would have taken up quite a bit of his time, since it was a new initiative and an important initiative as far as the Bosnian Serb leadership was concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Treanor, I wanted to include the BH -- SR BH Assembly, because he did have that job as well. But primarily, as your last answer suggested, primarily I was thinking of his position as the Speaker of the Serb Assembly, because, again, the position is this, isn't it, that, as you rather implied, a brand new body, with its own brand new Rules of Procedure, at a time of intense activity, was inevitably going to require an enormous amount of time for the Speaker, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- I would think it was going to take up -- it was going to be a busy period for him, but inevitably enormous, I don't know. But it was clearly -- it was an important job that had to be done, and he was the one that was doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Treanor, you weren't there. You've seen voluminous documentation and can form some sort of view based simply on the scale of the documentation and the type of issues that were resolved. Perhaps I can put it this way. Being Speaker of the Serb Assembly from late 1991 onwards must have been a full-time job, mustn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I don't know what a full-time job is, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Easy to recognise --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that his days were very busy. I don't really think that a sharp distinction can be drawn among the various tasks and matters that many of these individuals were involved in and make a clear distinction between, well, this is work on the Assembly, this is work in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. government, this is work in the party, this is work in the Political Council. I don't think that they structured their work days that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Treanor, I'm not going to make such an unrealistic suggestion to you as that people ask compartmentalise their work in such an extreme way. I have your answer in relation to whether it was a full-time job. Do you know -- for example, do you know where the Speaker of the Assembly worked, this being Mr. Krajisnik, of course?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe his office was in the Assembly building in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where Dr. Karadzic's office was?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his party office was in the Holiday Inn, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was a completely -- obviously it's a hotel. It's a completely different building from the Assembly. How far away is that from the Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's only a matter of a couple hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can follow almost literally your conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very interesting, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm glad Your Honour found it interesting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we take, please, the intercept binder now. [Microphone not activated] This is a -- sorry. Tab 20?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 20, conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Dukic. And we're in November 1991. And then towards the foot of the page, we get about ten lines up: On Thursday, the 21st. Do you see that? That's Mr. Dukic speaking. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Which page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's on the first page.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first page. Toward the bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About ten lines up: On Thursday, the 21st at 2.00, we have our Deputies' Club, isn't that right? Yes, there will be an assembly, an assembly at 2.00. Yes, our assembly, but I mean it's like the Deputies' Club. At 2.00. Yes. Please I suggest we have a meeting at the party Main Board at 12.00 and Radovan agrees with it. And then they go over the page. And then at the top of the next page, Mr. Dukic says: Because, you see, there are some things -- there's the referendum report. I don't see 50 per cent of the deputies are also members of the Main Board or the other way around, and I think you commented in your evidence, you dealt with this at page 1480 to 1481. You commented. You thought it was probably about a third. The -- when -- what do you understand what is meant by the reference to: Yes, our assembly, but I mean it's like the Deputies' Club. Can you say what it is Mr. Dukic is meaning by that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Krajisnik is speaking at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Yes, it is Mr. Krajisnik. I beg your pardon. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's, I believe, referring to the fact that almost all of the members of the Bosnian Serb Assembly were members of the Deputies' Club of the SDS and SPO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he's simply really saying -- is it really saying this: You don't really have to worry about technical distinctions about whether it's a meeting of the Deputies' Club or it's a session of the Assembly, because actually they're the same people? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think he's saying they're the same people. In fact, interestingly enough, we do continue to see a distinction made between meetings of the Deputies' Club and sessions of the Assembly, of the membership almost completely coincided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then at page 2, about ten lines on, because look here, you see Mr. Dukic is saying: Because, look here, we completely neglected the Main Board. I don't know whether the next phrase -- we see this all the time, and I'm just going to ask you to clarify. We see people all the time saying fuck this and fuck that and fuck the other. Is that equivalent in strength to the phrase which presumably comes up time and time again in B/C/S? This is not a very easy area for interpreters as it happens, so I'm just asking you whether --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's my impression that in certain circles, certainly in that country, the use of that expression is a lot looser than the equivalent expression is in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I see. Well, I think that's really answering my question. So that seems to indicate it's rather milder, it's rather more freely used, is what you're saying. Of course, it's less consternation than it might do.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It depends on the situation. For instance, I don't see Dr. Plavsic using that a lot in her conversations with Dr. Karadzic. So I think the degree of formality of the conversation and the relationship between the individuals speaking enters into it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, well, it's not a major point, Mr. Treanor, but it does come up about a million times in the papers, so ... So anyway, with that phrase coming up again, we completely neglected the Main Board. And then Mr. Krajisnik [indiscernible]. Then Mr. Dukic says: The people have not got together for a year. You know what it's like. They are calling and asking and what's going on. And then Mr. Krajisnik: No, the Main Board has to function. And then

utterances.speaker: MR. DUKIC
utterances.text: See here, it's the main -- the party's main body. It can't listen. First we'll clear up the political situation a bit. Do you -- you've done a very extensive study of the documentation in this case. Would it be a fair summary to say that Mr. Krajisnik's approach to matters generally was to want them to be done properly, constitutionally, legally, procedurally, correctly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think he was aware of the niceties, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not just aware of them. After all, I suggest you must have formed a clear impression of this, Mr. Treanor, because this case is, after all, a very major prosecution of Mr. Krajisnik and that's what we're here for and you've been reading these documents for many years. So you must have formed an impression as to whether what I've just put to you is correct, that Mr. Krajisnik, and just to clarify, that Mr. Krajisnik was somebody who was -- I might as well quote what I said before, his approach to matters generally was to want them to be done properly, constitutionally, legally and procedurally [sic], correctly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that my impression is that Mr. Krajisnik is somebody that knows how to use the system, that knows how to use it to get done what he wants to get done, someone who knows how to manipulate the system, if you will. I thought you might be going a different place with your question about this passage. I notice that it's Rajko Dukic whose the chairman of the Executive Board who suggests having a meeting of the Main Board. Mr. Dukic is a bit of a stickler. He's a businessman. I think that's why they made him head of the Executive Committee, to make sure that things got done. And here he's talking to Mr. Krajisnik who is a member of the Main Board suggesting that they have a meeting of the Main Board which hasn't met in over a year and which is apparently a matter that really hasn't bothered Mr. Krajisnik at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you can't quite go that far, can you, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it hasn't apparently bothered them in the last year and he's only gotten around to it since Mr. Dukic pointed out to him, and they said, yes, of course, we have to have a Main Board meeting. But he seems to have been very happy to operate over the previous year, or at least since July 1991, when he -- it may only have been at that date that he became a member of the Main Board, without having meetings of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On a more general point, Mr. Treanor, the -- I take it that in the course of preparing for this case, you have, for example -- well, you've read the indictment against Mr. Krajisnik, have you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite honestly, I don't think I have ever read any of the versions of the indictment against Mr. Krajisnik from beginning to end, and probably what I ever read of it was the first version of the indictment, which I understand has been replaced many times since then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you haven't read the indictment, what, if any, other documents specifically relating to this case against Mr. Krajisnik have you read?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean legal documents?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean legal documents?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I should -- thank you. Perhaps we should refine it first in that sense. Yes, legal documents, such as pre-trial briefs.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had a look - I certainly didn't read from cover to cover - at the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, in particular, sections which were related to the subject matter of our report. And I similarly had a look - but again did not read from cover to cover - at the Defence's pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So anything else in the -- so far as filed legal documentation is concerned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I'm not sure what else there would be, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can promise you, there's other stuff, Mr. Treanor. What about any evidential material, statements of witnesses or potential witnesses, prospective witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the framework of your question? Temporally and case-wise? Well, I've been working here for ten years, so I have seen witness statements. I quite frankly do not make it a practice to read witness statements. In fact, I sort of make it a practice not to read witness statements, because, among other things, I don't have time to do that. I'm more interested in the documents, and I'm interested in finding out what I can from the documents and not being influenced by things that the witnesses may say. It's a practical matter as well. I do not have time to read both. That being said, I have seen witness statements over the years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have from time to time been involved in --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have very occasionally taken part in interviews, particularly during a mission to Pale in -- well, I guess there were two missions; one in very late 1997 and one in early 1998. That was the mission during which Mr. Krajisnik was interviewed. There have been a couple of other occasions in which I have sat in on witness interviews, not in relation to this particular case, I don't believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a point arising out of a question and answer a few minutes ago. The SDS headquarters in the Holiday Inn were in fact about three kilometres away from the Assembly. Those are my instructions, Mr. Treanor. Could that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be. Could be. I haven't -- I haven't measured it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's something I'll have to clear up and come back to there, because there's some discrepancy about dates. But I'm not going to take the Tribunal's and Mr. Treanor's time by trying to sort that out this very second. I'll come back to that if necessary, and if there's any correction required, I shall make that. Mr. Treanor, you gave some evidence in relation to the -- by now fairly well-known documents or document described as Variants A and B?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to dwell on that in great detail right now, but what you did say in your evidence, and this is at page 1507 of the transcript, you said -- there were two things you'd like to point out on the basis of previous documents that we've seen in the course of your evidence. One is that you believed that the document had been distributed at a meeting of the Main Board of the SDS on the 20th of December, and then you based that on the fact that -- you said: We see various parts of the document being implemented very soon after that date. The -- is the position that you -- well, clearly personally you weren't there, but that based on your reading of the documents, despite that inference, you actually don't have any reliable knowledge of when and how that document came to be distributed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documentarily, no. Certainly, the documents are -- I think we introduced all the documents. That is an inference based on the documents. I think it's a reasonable inference. The variant A and B documents dated the 19th of December, we know from the Grkovic diary that there was a large party meeting, I believe at the Holiday Inn, on the 20th. There was a session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 21st, which involved a lot of the same people that came to the meeting on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first Crisis Staff, of which we have definite knowledge of when it was formed, was formed on the 23rd of December, which I believe was a Monday. So in fact, that would have been -- appears that it would have been the first opportunity to have called a local meeting to form a Crisis Staff after the 19th of December and after those other meetings took place, hence the conclusion that it was distributed during that period and most likely at the meeting on the 20th, which was a party meeting at the session of the Assembly. It doesn't make any reference to distributing such a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that Crisis Staff of which you say you have definite knowledge of when -- was that Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's more than one, and I would only be speaking from memory. It may have been Bratunac. I think there may have been another one, but certainly there was at least one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's just you refer to the first Crisis Staff, singular. If you want to correct that, then of course --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I'm speaking from memory. There may have been more than one, and there were others formed in days shortly thereafter, before the end of the year, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so when you -- when you said in your evidence, and I don't know whether I gave the page reference, 1507 of the transcript, when you said that you based your inference of distribution of the document on the fact that you saw various parts of the document being implemented very soon after that date, that's what you're talking about there, this --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your references a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say: It's clear -- well, you say numerous numbered copies of this document. How numerous are the, roughly speaking, how numerous are the numbered copies that you have of this variant A and B document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they're all listed in a footnote in the report. I don't know the exact number. I think we're getting up to 10 or 12. Again, there's a footnote. I could locate the footnote and count them. But I think it's in, you know, the 10, 12, 15 area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we both have to try and work from memory of your footnote, Mr. Treanor. So but we've -- but it's in that ballpark, anyway?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, it's not 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. No. That's helpful.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it's more than -- it's certainly more than one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are they at this particular moment?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those documents?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're in the evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just -- physically where?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Evidence Unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the originals are physically where? It's just a simple practical question, Mr. Treanor, because I don't know the answer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's a simple practical question that was just answered twice. Mr. Treanor indicated it was in the Evidence Unit. If you're asking physically where that's located --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the confusion is whether we are talking about the originals or certified copies or just copies. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Actually, partly the simple confusion was I didn't pick up the word "unit", and so when the witness said, "They're in the evidence," that was why I then asked a couple of times, because in the evidence can mean ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He should clarify. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My apologies. I didn't pick up the word "unit". So no doubt we don't need to take time here sorting out where the Evidence Unit is. That could be worked out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, that material is presumably readily obtainable if we want to see it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, if I can add, I'm under the impression that copies have been made of all the documents that are referred to in the report and provided to Defence and the Trial Chamber. So ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I very much expect they have. But there's no thrust of complaint or criticism. But sometimes original documents are something worth looking at and I just wanted from a practical point of view to see where they were. Thank you. That's a very helpful answer. Thank you. And then you pointed out in your evidence there's no direct reference in the records of the Assembly session of any distribution of that document. And in fact, it's correct, isn't it, that there's no -- there's no direct record, minutes or notes of any meeting of any organ or body of distribution of that document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The only reference we have, the only knowledge of the meeting on the 20th, comes from the diary entry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's also -- there's no -- it's connected, really, but there's no record of any such document having been -- or its contents having been formally adopted or approved by any organ of the SDS or --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or the Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I could just add to the question about the whereabouts of the Variant A and B document, just to be perfectly clear we're talking about the same thing. Such copies of those documents as we have are in the Evidence Unit. What the status of those particular copies is vis-a-vis are they original, the original documents that were recovered somewhere in the field or are they copies of those documents or certified copies of those documents, I couldn't say at this time. But that can easily be determined from the records of the Evidence Unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may at this point seek some clarification within the terms of 90(H), and I was trying to divine from the questions precisely what the Defence case was with respect to this particular document. I think 90(H) obviates the need to make that effort and that should be made clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see on the transcript it says "98(H)", where you referred to 90(H).

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, 90(H), requires you, if you are not sticking strictly to the subject matter of examination-in-chief, to put to the witness what your case is in respect of the matter you are raising with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, yes. Even without the number, I certainly am proposing to do that. However, I'm going to come back to Variants A and B in the course of my cross-examination rather than pursue it to the end now. But Your Honour can rest assured that our case will be put so far as it properly needs to be put to Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question is to what extent it properly needs to be put, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that is the question, Your Honour, because there are distinct limits to how far strictly anything needs to be put to a witness who was not there, who has no firsthand knowledge, and is just here to tell us and explain what's in the documentation and put it into context. However, I'm not necessarily going to adopt a minimalist approach to the application of the Rules in relation to the putting of my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although I do not see any limitation in Rule 90(H), where it reads: "In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears, which is in contradiction of the evidence given by that witness." I just repeat what exactly is in Rule 90(H). I wouldn't say that in every respect it's easy to apply and easy to interpret, but in my view, it's -- but perhaps we could discuss it over the break with the Judges that to put the case of the Defence in a situation should not be done at the end but rather when starting asking questions on that subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I would certainly want --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I'd certainly like to think about that, but if I say I'd like to think about it, that's exactly what I mean. I'd like to think about it. I'm not saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you're not pursuing the matter at this very moment, then I'd like to give you some time to think about it, and whenever you revisit the issue, that you have a clear opinion on how to apply this Rule and whether we then agree with you or not is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do. I could suggest, I have some fairly, well, views, forensically views as an advocate I do have some submissions and views about it. First of all, so far as the precise timing is concerned of when the case is put, I would follow the perfectly general principle that matters must be put to a witness in a way that's favour to the witness. So to ask questions in a way that the witness can't really fairly understand by saving up putting the case until the end of the questions wouldn't be a fair way of dealing with it. Apart from that, subject to that principle of fairness, the precise timing as to when the case is put I'd suggest is pretty much in the hands of the advocate as long as it's done in the course of the cross-examination. As a matter of fact, the citation, I don't have the Rule in front of me, but it turns out actually that my recollection of it in my own head was pretty reasonably accurate as Your Honour cited it. The limitation or the limitations really are pretty much inherent in the first few words of that Rule, that it's, so far as the -- now I'm not remembering in detail, but the -- so far as the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the Defence case. Because in this particular case, actually, that would be likely to be far more restrictive in Mr. Treanor's case of what I would be required to put to him than I would in practice actually put. So I doubt there's going to be a problem, because my inclination following naturally with a certain amount of cultural baggage that I bring with me as to how these things are done, my inclination will be to put to Mr. Treanor probably slightly more than would absolutely strictly be required under that Rule. So if we do run into problems, we do, but I think perhaps we could cross that bridge, Your Honour, when we come to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you are now pursuing another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I'm going to come back to Variants A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I don't think it would have any use now to ask from the Defence to put to the witness what would be dealt with only at a later stage. Yes, I see you're nodding. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just say that I don't believe that there's been any unfairness so far in the way that I've put any questions to the witness or any difficulty for him in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took it that Mr. Tieger wanted to prevent this to happen. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Nothing like getting your retaliation in first, as we say, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. There was something I just wanted to mention. Yes. And, Your Honour, it may very well of course clearly my questions about where these documents are physically located that we might take the trouble to get hold of those documents before proceeding with this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We moved on in your evidence in chief, then, Mr. Treanor, and you were referring to a document at -- in bundle 6, and we're back to the main files rather than the transcript or speeches file.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope Your Honours -- do you say you have number 6 in court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least we have one copy here, and we could share it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at tab 68, minutes from the 4th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People. That's the 21st of December, so that's among the meetings that we were just talking about. And at page 24, we've got Mr. Brdjanin talking. You had cited the passage at page 24 about three paragraphs down: We know very well that the Serbian people want a state ruled by law, a state that has its laws, but at the same time, we can see for ourselves that Europe does not recognise that, since Europe apparently understands only force, I think that force must be responded to with force, thus I urge us to stop pledging ourselves to -- and that presumably serfdom rather than Serbdom, is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm checking. There is a concept of Serbdom, which I don't know if that word exists in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's the totality of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So it is pledging ourselves to Serbdom. Yes, I see. Serbdom. And instead, I call upon Serbs in Sarajevo, [indiscernible] and Northern Bosnia to heed the call for mobilisation so we can defend our western border. Once we have secured our borders, Europe will accept the facts. And you said that that in particular, that portion, reflected what you described as this ongoing tension. This is at page 1516 of the transcript. If not outright military hostilities in Croatia. And you said in your evidence: I'm not sure exactly what the military situation in Croatia was at this point. Well, probably without being flippant, nobody knew exactly what it was because nobody ever does really with a military situation. But what what was in its essentials at that time, Mr. Treanor, the military situation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really sure. I mean, what I was referring to is the fact that there were discussions going underway under international auspices which did result at the beginning of January in the adoption of the so-called Vance Plan for Croatia. So how active the fighting was per se at this particular point in time, I don't know. And I think I'm trying to indicate that maybe it was -- it was winding down a bit in view of the fact that the negotiations were coming to a conclusion. There had, of course, been numerous ceasefires and they had been broken and repeatedly, that sort of thing. But how active the fighting was at this particular time, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they were on the -- we needn't go into enormous detail of this, but they were on the verge of agreement in relation to Croatia, weren't they, and there was an agreement in January and UNPROFOR was then established, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And agreed to by the parties in relation to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At this particular point in time, there may have been an expectation -- not an unreasonable expectation on the part of certain people, including Mr. Brdjanin, that hostilities might in fact continue or flare up again or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you this, Mr. Treanor: We could no doubt go through dozens, hundreds, perhaps, of passages in the various minutes, which are pretty extensive, but your impression from all the documents that you've read, including the quite voluminous minutes of various sessions and Serb Assembly and so on, does it support the conclusion that the members of the Serb Assembly - let's take the most numerous body - were at all points a very difficult group of people to control and keep in check?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would certainly say that they spoke their mind and the discussions are very interesting. And differences of opinion certainly arise. I would say, however, that, in my impression, and I believe that's what you're asking me for, is my impression --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- over reading these things, that especially in the early period, and by the early period, I would say I mean through the middle, say, of 1992, almost everything gets passed. It's put on the agenda. There might be a lot of discussion and some amendments, that sort of thing, but at the end of the day, the agenda items do in fact get passed and they seem to be passed virtually unanimously. There are certain points where Mr. Krajisnik does say: Okay. We'll save this for later and that sort of thing. But if by difficult to control you mean they would not accept, at this period in time, the proposals that were put before them by the -- whoever it was, the Council of Ministers or a report by Dr. Karadzic, et cetera, they almost invariably did accept them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout this whole period -- we're focusing largely, but not entirely, but focusing largely on what was happening within the organs of the SDS and then the Serb Assembly and so on. Throughout this whole period, international negotiations were continuing, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of one sort of another, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of one sort or another?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, rather generally at the moment, but on the documentation that you've seen, the Bosnian Serb leadership were not, in late 1991 and through the first three or four months of 1992, they were not seeking to sabotage those negotiations, were they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by "sabotage". I think that they -- and by "they" I mean the negotiating team as presented in their reports to the Assembly, negotiating team consisting of Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Koljevic, and Mr. Krajisnik primarily, seemed hopeful that they would be able to get what they wanted through negotiation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in a sense, Mr. Treanor, you have -- you have correctly defined for the purpose of your answer my use of the word "sabotage". So but then to make it clear: The --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are some tactical issues, perhaps, which I don't find much light on in these documents. But, you know, for instance, you see in the press and elsewhere perhaps, they have accepted this particular proposal because they know the other side won't accept it and so then the onus will be on the other side for having rejected it, you know, that sort of game. But not being able to speak to that, I would say that one certainly does get the impression, especially during the course of the -- of February and early March, that the Bosnian Serb negotiating team seem very hopeful indeed that they would be able to reach their goals through negotiation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly, Mr. Treanor, we can probably agree what you describe as, well, we ask for something that we know they will refuse so they will be in a bad light and so on. There's nothing to distinguish this part of the world, former Yugoslavia, from any other part of the world, where that's all part and parcel of normal negotiating tactics, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's -- that's in the -- that's in the basket of negotiating tactics. That's certainly true, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you, of course, have the considerable advantage of not just having read all the public stuff and no doubt the media stuff about the negotiations, but of course we have all this documentation showing what was going on back at home in the Assembly and in the various meetings. So that's the advantage that you've got. So in a nutshell, is it fair to say that there's no indication of -- at all of any sabotage in a sense of it being a conflict between the position adopted in the negotiations internationally and what was happening back in former Yugoslavia, with it being just a transparent ruse to get negotiations to break down?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. In fact, what -- and getting back a little bit to your earlier question, what we see is the negotiating team trying to assure the deputies that the negotiations were going well, they were progressing, they were making progress toward their goals, in spite of some reservations that certain people may have had, in particular, an important point that they were not getting in -- that emerged in the second half of February and certainly continued, was the idea of remaining within Yugoslavia. This was the Suma, if I can put it that way, in many respects, of Bosnian Serb policy and politics. Hence the sharp reaction to the platform of the memorandum, the establishment of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, the holding of the plebiscite, all of which I laid out in my presentation in the relevant documents. The plebiscite thereafter came to be a very important catchword in discussions in the Assembly. Constant references back to the plebiscite. The Serbian people have spoken in the plebiscite what they want and that is what we are bound to seek to achieve. As I say, toward the end of February, it became clear that that was not going to be achievable immediately and the negotiating team had to, if you will, sell that to the delegates, which they managed to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've exactly anticipated my next question with your use of the word "sell," Mr. Treanor. Is it your impression from the documents that the leadership who had been involved in the negotiations were constantly involved in a very difficult exercise of leading the rank and file, if I can call them that, of the Assembly to feel that progress was being made in the negotiations, that that line should continue to be pursued, although in fact things were being lost along the way?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the beginning of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Is it your impression from the documents that the leadership, SDS Serb leadership who had been involved in these international negotiations, were constantly involved in a very difficult exercise of leading the rank and file of the Assembly to feel that progress was being made, so that that line of negotiations should be pursued, even though, of course, from time to time the leadership knew that they were losing things in the negotiation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. They were involved in what appears to have been a rather difficult process all around, the negotiations on the one hand and going back to the Assembly, on the other. They were able to bring the Assembly along, it is my impression, because of the confidence that the members of the Assembly had in the negotiating team, in particular, the confidence that they had in Mr. Krajisnik, who, it is my impression, was one of the most outspoken advocates of the Yugoslav line, if I can put it that way. That is, that the ultimate goal is to be part of Yugoslavia, or whatever the state of the -- of all the Serbs will be called, and we are not giving up on that goal. We cannot achieve it now, for tactical reasons. But trust me, we're still headed in that direction. We're not selling out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we move on? We're in file 6. Could we go to section 74, tab 74, please. I beg your pardon. No, I think I actually might want to move on to the next file.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's number 7. I don't know whether that would mean that perhaps that's a convenient point for the Tribunal to have the break. I'm entirely in Your Honour's hands, of course, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You finally are. We'll have a break until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the mail has arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I remember when first-class mail was introduced in a certain country that it always went slower than second-class mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's in some book or other cleft sticks are sometimes used for carrying documents backwards and forwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might as well hand them up. I did bring three copies of the letter with me, so you can't have too much of a good thing, Your Honour, so I will hand them up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, quality rather than quantity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Both, Your Honour. [Previous translation continues]... microphone when I say we aim for both. It does contain at the back, just for the record, Your Honour, the fax transmission sheet, which confirms when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor -- should I say, Your Honour, I have received what I accept as entirely justified complaints about going too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm aware of it and I am also aware of your answer, which is cooperative and not being offended if you're reminded to the speed of your speech. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I think also it's helpful if I go really slowly now, it's helpful if I leave a little bit more of a gap. Or perhaps, Mr. Treanor, there was no criticism of you, but I think between us if we leave a little bit more of a gap between questions and answers for them. But I think I'm the culprit here really, so ... Or was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, could we take -- we'll need 6 and 7 here, but if we could just take volume 6, please, 74. And again, my apologies. I'm afraid I'm not in a position to give at every point the cross-reference to the page in the B/C/S version. I've acknowledged the point and we'll do our best in future. But I apologise. I'm not able to do that this morning. I don't have those cross-references. So my apologies to the interpreters there. But page 12, you drew attention, Mr. Treanor, to comments of Mr. Leovac and then Professor Nadanovic [phoen], who said: We can split up on the basis of the recent census what happens to Serbs in Croatia. The army must conquer Osijek and Sisak to compensate for the deficiency within national borders. A confederation is the minimum we must demand, and we did not define the maximum, what are our maximum borders. We need a single Serbian state which cannot be inhabited by Muslims because they would overwhelm us with their birth rate. Now, the first point here is this is, would you agree, Mr. Treanor, this is a pretty good example of a rather hawkish member, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that these -- this represents a rather maximalist view how -- if you want to equate that with hawkish, you may. Whether -- and I think there was another part to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you're giving evidence, Mr. Treanor, so if you present it, don't adopt my --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: How common -- how common this view may have been relative to other people is a little bit harder to gauge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. The -- then the second point is this: That he refers in the last sentence to needing a single Serbian state which cannot be inhabited by Muslims. So that's a strongish view, isn't it, on that point? Does that come within your definition of maximalist?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he talks about, wherever it leads, he talks about: Because they would overwhelm us with their birth rate. Now, as a simple fact, Mr. Treanor, it is correct, isn't it, that the Muslim birth rate was substantially higher than the Serb birth rate at this time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a demographer. This is a complex issue. I think what I can say on that issue, and I believe what I present to the Court, is the fact that that was certainly a widespread perception among the leadership of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in your -- the material that you put before the Court in bundle 7 -- we can go to tab 83. In the first place, I'm going to have to ask you, Mr. Treanor, to remind us, by which I mean me, among other things, exactly what this particular document is.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe this document is an update of a previous report that was done with the same title. The previous report is dated, I believe, September 1991. And this document appears to be an update on that report, prepared at the request of the Bosnian Serb Council of Ministers in January 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at page 9 of the same document, we see a graph, don't we, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. headed, "Demographic trends of the BH population"? Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to put to you any question which you can't fairly be expected to answer. So I'll put it this way: Have you seen any material in the course of your examination of all the documentation in connection with this case which is significantly inconsistent with what we -- the pattern that we see in that graph or that chart at page 9?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what we see here is a, I may say, a rather crude analysis of population trends. I say crude because I have seen in other cases certainly reports prepared by our demographers. They are a lot more complex than this. As far as comparing this to any other document that I've seen, the only documents that I've looked at in this connection are the documents produced by the Bosnian Serbs, and I don't recollect anything among their papers that's at great variance to this. I think that is the point I was trying to make presenting the document, that this was their view of population trends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you've referred to more sophisticated -- that wasn't your exact word, but I'm sure that's the gist of it, to more sophisticated demographic reports which you have seen in connection with other cases, presumably.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I probably have seen the one for this case as well, since it was produced in my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, so based on that, then, my question would be: Have you any reason, based on everything you've seen in relation to the demography of Bosnia in the late '80s and the early '90s, 1990s, have you seen anything which is inconsistent with the basic proposition that the Muslim birth rate was and birth rate projections were significantly above those for the other nationalities?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me to recollect what I've seen in a very complex report, one which I certainly did not read from cover to cover, and if I did, I'm quite confident that I would not have understood a lot of it because of its technical nature. My recollection is that the differences in the rate of population growth were not that great. But that is a report that I believe is before this Trial Chamber, so I'm a bit reluctant to say more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Treanor, I don't want to -- that's very fair if you -- there's limits of what you feel confident of saying. I'm not going to press you any further on that. The -- then on the same page, in bundle 6. Well, in fact, going over the page to page 13. Sorry. Are you there, Mr. Treanor? Dr. Milos Blazic: How can we secure economic foundations for our republic? What are the consequences of the influx of refugees from Croatia to BH?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Have I lost you? Tab 74, bundle 6.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the page number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 74. And then it's the last page.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 13th. It is the very last page in 74.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Professor Leovac: There will have to be a detailed discussion -- well, I'll start again. Mr. Blazic, Dr. Blazic: How can we secure economic foundations for our republic? What are the consequences of the influx of refugees from Croatia to BH? And then Professor Leovac: There will have to be a detailed discussion about this in the future. Proclaim a Serbian republic of BH as soon as possible. Form an analytical group for determining the overall Serbian borders in BH. Set the record clear with the army. What does it want? And then Professor Leovac: Representatives of the council should talk to the SDA president and the president of the Assembly of the Serbian People. We should talk to Krajisnik tomorrow and settle this immediately. And of course the president of the Assembly is Mr. Krajisnik. The council is -- because that's what this whole section is dealing with. The council is the Political Council, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you, in the evidence that you gave earlier in this case, and this is at page 1528 of the transcript, you cited that passage and then you -- well, in fact, Mr. Tieger quoted that passage. And then you answered: Yes. This is a reflection of who the council perceives to be the two most important leaders among the Bosnian Serb leadership. Mr. Treanor, the -- expressed in that very general, fairly sweeping way that they are the two most important leaders among the Bosnian Serb leadership, it's part of my obligation to put my case, I'm not going to remotely suggest that Mr. Krajisnik was unimportant. That would be ridiculous. But it doesn't necessarily follow from this particular exchange and this particular issue that Mr. Krajisnik overall was one of the two most important leaders among the Bosnian Serb leadership, does it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view, it indicates that. They're discussing some very important matters here, and they seem to want to pursue the matter further, and they want to go right to the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, isn't it here also importantly a question of what actually needs to be done so that if you are going to, as Professor Leovac suggests, you're going to proclaim a Serbian republic of BH as soon as possible, and then you're going to form a group for determining the overall Serbian borders, there are two particular responsibilities of Mr. Krajisnik which are bound to bring him in for this issue: One is, and obviously, his speakership or Presidency of the Assembly, because it's bound to involve the Assembly and procedures in the Assembly, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at some point it certainly would, and in fact it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So what I'm saying is it's just absolutely obvious on this particular issue, formation of the Serbian republic for one thing, on this particular issue. Being the Speaker of the Assembly, in practice, he's got to be involved, hasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it gets back to an approach that we've seen before, where you see some inevitability about something. I'm afraid I'll have to admit to the Trial Chamber that in my world view, certainly in history and politics, unlike death and taxes, nothing is inevitable. There are always choices to be made, there are different personalities involved. Some people perform well in the functions they hold, some don't. Some people become important despite the fact that they don't have particular functions. And I think Mr. Krajisnik is somebody who did well at his job. Other people recognise that, people in his political party, including Dr. Karadzic, who he was otherwise close to. And therefore, they looked to him for leadership and guidance. If he had been a different person, or if a different person had been the chairman or the president, I'm sorry, we call him president of the Assembly, that might not have been the case. They might have said: Well, talk to Mr. Krajisnik -- I mean, they could have said the same thing except not the president of the Assembly, but let's talk to the president of the Deputies' Club, Mr. Krajisnik, if Mr. Krajisnik had been the president of the Deputies' Club and Mr. Maksimovic had been the president of the Assembly and they were perceived in different ways by different people, then this could be different. As I say, there's no inevitability about anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's this. I want to try to -- let's say narrow, but identify such differences as there might be between us, Mr. Treanor. The -- and more generally, it may be helpful if I make it absolutely clear. I've already said that it's no part of the Defence case that Mr. Krajisnik wasn't important. That would be just ludicrous. It is so you and everybody else understands the Defence case that Mr. Krajisnik was good at his job. Whether he would say it himself, that's the case I'm putting on his behalf, that he was good at his job. In fact, very good at his job.
