He was -- and I'm talking about the job as Speaker, president of the Assembly, as, if you like, his principal position. It's also the defence case that Mr. Krajisnik was -- he was a popular person. You speak of parliaments all over the world tend to have that characteristic, don't they, which helps them to get into the job and do it. That's broadly correct, Mr. Treanor, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the position of Speaker, as you put it, is a different position in different countries, has a different quality in different political systems, which is why we refer in our report to the president of the Assembly, not to confuse that office with the office of Speaker in the United Kingdom or the nature of the office of Speaker of the House of Representatives in the United States, which are two different things indeed. Whether those particular individuals are popular and who they're popular with, I think is a subject for discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you specifically, Mr. Treanor: Is it apparent to you, from the documentation, maybe there were people that didn't like him, but is it apparent to you from all the documentation you've read that Mr. Krajisnik was very broadly a popular figure within the Assembly and the SDS membership?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if by the Assembly you mean the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I do mean that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I would qualify him as being a very respected leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, respected and, so far as one could tell from the documentation, Mr. Treanor, respected and generally liked?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he may have been with -- with all candidness, I didn't quite get the being -- the liked and loved bit out of what I read, but I certainly did get the respect part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, you added the loved bit, Mr. Treanor, there. But I'm not going to press you on that. But if you don't get from the documentation what I put to you, then that's a fair answer. You don't get that. But it's my case, which is also what I was doing, it's my case on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik that he was generally well-liked among the SDS membership, that he was -- certainly he was respected, that he was very good at his job and that, in particular, and I just invite your comment as to whether this is an impression which you have been able to gain from the documentation, that he was -- he was a pretty effective fixer in the perfectly good political sense.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, and the impression I have, is he was very effective, he was respected. He may have been liked. Just not one -- in the impressions I gathered, I'm not disputing that, it's just not one of the impressions that was made on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that in fact what you referred to earlier of -- you said earlier this morning that -- either everything, perhaps you said, or practically everything which was put on the agenda for the Serb Assembly got passed.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And quite often in parliamentary bodies, things get consistently passed as a result of good judgement as to what to put on the agenda in the first place, coupled with sound and assiduous preparatory work before you actually get to the session itself.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, undoubtedly many factors that go into the adoption of any particular decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's normal politics, isn't it, that it's --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, and I'm not trying to dispute that. What's in the back of my mind is that what's going on here is not a normal situation. This is a -- from the Bosnian Serb point of view, a very severe crisis situation, and I think one of the factors that enters into the consensus - that's the wrong word. One of the factors that enters into the adoption of all the measures that I referred to during this period is that there was a consensus on how to confront this crisis and how to surmount it, what the steps taken should be. Later on, after they get the republic established and they start getting into economic issues, privatisation, all that sort of thing, then you see differences starting to emerge. But as far as their primary national interests and how to protect them and advance them, I think there was a large -- very, very large degree of consensus on that, and that is one of the factors that enabled so many of these measures to be passed with very brief discussion at many of the sessions, which is not to say that I believe that Mr. Krajisnik didn't handle the Assembly effectively. I think he did handle it effectively. That's another element in this situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout -- when I say this period, and really, I'm talking, say, October 1991 through to April 1992. Let's take that six-month period. Throughout that six-month period, there was, as I think you've indicated yourself earlier, there was constant activity for the Serb Assembly, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by "constant". By constant you mean continuous. No, it wasn't continuous. We know when the sessions were. They weren't every day. They were certainly more frequent than they were during the months after April, and there was undoubtedly a lot of preparatory work to be done, and this, that, and the other thing. So there was a period of intense activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: See, having indicated to you, I hope clearly, and covered the basic ground what the Defence case is in this area. Accepting that Mr. Krajisnik was certainly important as president, and I'll stick with that terminology, as president of the Assembly, once we start to move into other areas of activity and to face it head on, once we start to move into the situation of extreme conflict in 1992 and once we get into an area which therefore involves military activity and other organs, it's too sweeping to say that Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were the two most important leaders among the Bosnian Serb leadership. It's too much of an oversimplification, isn't it, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to a particular period now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I refer to the -- yes, all right. We move on towards -- let's -- I was still referring to the whole of that period, but if we look at the situation in February, March, April, where, we'd agree, it was really reaching crisis point, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at that situation, and we look at the -- all the issues, including the -- obviously the escalating military questions which were coming up, it's simply too sweeping to say: Yes, the two most important leaders were Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik? I should say I'm not disputing Mr. Karadzic as one of the two most important. That also would be ludicrous. But as far as Mr. Krajisnik is concerned.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only qualifier I would put on that would be that they continued to be the two most important civilian political leaders. Obviously, after the conflict broke out, especially after the establishment of the army, military leaders got to be very important indeed. But as civilian political leaders, my impression is that they continued to be the two most important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think to some extent we can see this from your report and your evidence, but I wonder, Mr. Treanor, whether you could indicate to the Tribunal the extent to which you have or haven't in your review of the documentation examined the military aspects of the situation, and I'm talking particularly about the military actions of Serbs in February, March, April, May 1992.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have examined very few military documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that because they were largely not available or because you broadly didn't regard that as part of your remit for your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in order to write this report which plainly has been in a process of gestation since long before Mr. Krajisnik was indicted, was your report written in response to an instruction received at some point from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I take what you mean by written and report to mean the report that has been submitted in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I do, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated earlier, the origins of this report go back to the end of 1994, when I commenced doing research and writing on the subject of the Bosnian Serb leadership and utilising such documents as were available to us at that time and continuing over a period of years to develop that. So that work -- there was a work in progress, let me put it that way. There came to be a point in time when this trial team was interested, so they told me, interested in filing a report that would deal with the Serbian Democratic Party, how it was organised and functioned, and the other structures that were set up by the Bosnian Serb leadership during the period beginning in -- well, 1990 through the end of 1992. At that point, the pre-existing, if there's such a word, the existing draft was taken and added to and modified, and of course I think they gave us some desired parameters as far as length, which I apologise to the Court, I think we exceeded. So I think that pretty much answers the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So it was -- and, Mr. Treanor, I don't suggest there's anything surprising about this. So you had, if you like, your overall report, which had been worked on since 1994, in some form or another, anyway, and it was tailored, and I don't imply again anything in the least bit improper here, it was then tailored for the purposes of this case.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I stress, I'm not suggesting anything improper there.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would use the word "completed," perhaps. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After all, tailoring is not in itself a bad thing. So it was tailored for this particular case. So the point in time when this trial team, and the Prosecution trial team we're talking about, was interested in filing a report that would deal with the matters you've said, that was the subject of -- they expressed their interest to you, that was the subject of a formal communication to you, was it, a written communication: This is what we would like you and your team to do?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the nature of the communication, I don't think I would describe as formal. Not too many things get done in a formal manner. There were meetings, say, at which the issue was discussed. There wasn't a formal -- I don't believe that there was a formal sort of, you know, memorandum or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After all, at one end of the spectrum --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was, I've long forgotten and long ignored it. But I would describe it as being -- the request as being put informally, as I say, not embodied in some sort of formal document, but in the normal course of work, in discussion, and what not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as you're aware, there doesn't exist -- I think this follows from what you've said, but as far as you're aware, there doesn't exist a memorandum or letter or whatever in which the Prosecution say: Dear Mr. Treanor, please would you prepare a report covering the following matters and the following areas, 1, 2, 3, 4. No such memorandum?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall such a thing, which isn't to say it might not be there, but that would only be because I promptly forgot it, because I knew what was required in any case and went ahead with it and that sort of thing. But I just don't recall there being anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's something that's presumably --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, it wasn't something that I had next to me or members of my team had next to me as we were writing the report to make sure we were adhering to these -- whatever guidelines or something might have been in some formal paper of that description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I wouldn't suggest to you that that's what a team of experts would normally do, to keep the instructions at their elbow throughout the work. But the question of whether -- you said you don't remember. The question of whether there is somewhere a formal request to you and your team in writing, that's -- presumably that's something that's fairly readily checkable, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can look where, you know, where -- places where I look for things, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'd be grateful if -- I think I put these requests through the Tribunal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Treanor. If you'd look at those places where you'd expect to find such a thing. If it exists, then it would be highly appreciated if you would come back in the court and tell us whether you found anything and what you found.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could just clarify. What is it I'm looking for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking, as far as I understand, we're talking about a request in writing, because that's at least an object you could find, a request in writing indicating that you're requested to draft or write a report on certain subjects, whatever details therein.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Mr. Stewart used the word "formal, "however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking about memorandum a piece of -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. whatever has been put on paper in respect of a request asking you to write a report on the subjects covered by the report you have delivered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that to include email?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If printed out, it's email, and if it's not printed out and if you find something on your inbox, then we'd like you to print that out and consider it to be an object.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. That's most helpful, and that's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, so far as formal is concerned, I think I was simply probably wanting to draw a distinction between that and oral communication, which I'm not going to ask you to look for, surprisingly. I suppose I should say this: If actually what there is is a scrap of paper that says, you know, hey Pat, give us some stuff about Bosnia. Well, actually, in this context, yes, please, we would like to have it, but I don't seriously suppose that we're talking about that. So actually delete formal, please, and just substitute written, including email.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, does that seem fair?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Printed out. That makes it easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we then go on, please, to -- we're still in -- well, I think we've moved back to number 6, so can we go on, then, to volume 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was waiting for this opportunity. I didn't realise that so much time would pass between the small clarification I wanted to bring the Court's attention to and this moment. But at page 41, line 11, there is -- the transcript indicates a reference to the SDA in referring to a quotation by Professor Leovac. The document, however, indicates the SDS. And that's the document found at tab 74, page 13, I believe. I believe the line was: Professor Leovac, representatives of the council should talk to the SDS president. That was -- Mr. Stewart was simply reading from the document, and I think inadvertently substituted the word SDA for SDS at the page and line I indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It looks to me as if it was on line 13 rather than on 11, where I read: "And then Professor Leovac: Representatives of the council should talk to the SDA president. That's line 13, rather than 11, where it should be SDS, I take it. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'm grateful for the -- thank you. I'm grateful for the correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going on, then, to 7, file 7, bundle 7, page -- I'm sorry, tab 82. And then on page 5 -- I think it goes back to -- beg your pardon. On to page 6, paragraph 4. This was dealt with by you, Mr. Treanor. Page 1550, 1550 of the transcript earlier in evidence. And then you had highlighted paragraph 4, under questions and proposals. And I remind ourselves, this is a minute -- second meeting of the Ministerial Council of the Assembly. Mr. Krajisnik especially stressed the need to distribute the activities of the Assembly of the Serbian People of BH, its Ministerial Council and the Serbian Democratic Party of BH and its organs, in accordance with their competence. And you dealt with this in your evidence by saying this: That interesting remark by Mr. Krajisnik, interesting observation on the division of labour between the Assembly, the Ministerial Council, and the SDS. And then you say that Mr. Krajisnik may have apparently been feeling that the lines of authority were being crossed here and confusing. You describe this. Interesting is a word you use quite a lot, Mr. Treanor, in your evidence. What is the -- you've given evidence about this already, but I'm not quite clear. What is the particular point of interest here in this remark?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I find it interesting for two reasons, one general and one particular. In general, it indicates the perception of a very important player in the Bosnian Serb leadership of the state of affairs, if you will, within the structures they're setting up, reflecting a bit of confusion that's arising. They're setting up these new bodies and that sort of thing. And so their people are feeling their way as to what they should be doing and what they're doing, and he's saying that, well, you know, maybe we're getting a little confused here and we should be a little more rigid in distributing activities, as a general reflection of the state of business, if you will, within the new organs set up by the SDS. In particular, I found it interesting -- now, I thought I mentioned that, and if I didn't, I'll mention it now, although I can't remember the specific date of the documents. There is a document that emanates from the Executive Board of the SDS around this time, signed by Mr. Dukic, which is addressed to the Serbian ministries. Yes, I think that was the letter addressed to the ministries in the Bosnian Serb Ministerial Council about establishing relations with the corresponding ministries in the Republic of Serbia. And that document had always struck me as being interesting, if you will, as coming from a party organ, going to the new state organ. And I thought I had speculated in my testimony, if I'm allowed to speculate, that that may have been the type of thing that Mr. -- that may have struck Mr. Krajisnik as well. What's going in here? Why is the Executive Committee sending something to the Council of Ministers? That should be handled in a different matter, in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, the letter you're talking about -- you did refer to it in your evidence before, Mr. Treanor. That's absolutely right. The letter is convenient. It's in the same bundle. It's back at tab 80. That's -- we can -- that's the letter that you're talking about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to see whether this is in fact fairly limited. As I think you've commented yourself, in the fairly early stages of this rather radical new set-up, with the different, separate Serb organs, leading, of course, to declaration of Republika Srpska eventually. It's first of all not surprising that they were feeling their way, and it would be in a sense again very obviously Mr. -- part of Mr. Krajisnik's responsibility as president of the Assembly to make his contribution to having things efficiently run?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, there's no inevitability about anyone saying anything. But the point of presenting this, as indeed many of the other documents that I presented and you've raised is simply to show the Court what Mr. Krajisnik was doing and saying along the way. That's all. If I'd made a presentation, that theoretically would be possible, I suppose, without mentioning Mr. Krajisnik at all, I would imagine the Court would be sitting there thinking: Well ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would have been --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why do we need this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would have been a strange thing to do, Mr. Treanor. I think we can agree there. On the 11th of January, the Badinter -- I think it's Badinter Commission issued a report in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you give the Tribunal just a -- not much, I'm just asking a basic -- just a basic history of the establishment of the Badinter Commission and how that fitted in.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, off the top of my head, I believe it was in November, the end of November 1991, although it could have been December, the European economic -- no, the European Community, I guess, as it was then, the EC, having obviously been seized of the matter of the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia, adopted some guidelines, procedures, as to how they would deal with that issue, and in particular, the fact that they were being presented with requests from individual republics that the EC recognise their independence. And they wanted to satisfy -- when I say they, I mean the leaders of the EC, wanted to satisfy themselves that those republics had met certain minimum standards of democracy and, loosely put, respect for human rights. And they established this commission to review those applications for recognition and any other materials that may be submitted in that connection, and presumably they would have the right to ask for materials on their own, and then to offer an opinion to the members of the EC as to whether the individual republics had satisfied the requirements for recognition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Badinter -- well, he certainly had been a French minister. I think he had been a foreign minister of France; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he had been -- perhaps it isn't. But he had been a French minister, hadn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Badinter once was, and this is a fact of general knowledge, was the minister of justice of France.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Minister of justice. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. "Garde des sceaux", as it is said in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Merci bien. Yes. Minister of justice. And thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had -- you've cited the opinion in relation specifically of that commission in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The will of the peoples -- the commission indicates opinion that -- and this was 1555 of the transcript, the will of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina to constitute the SRBH, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a sovereign and independent state cannot be held to have been fully established. This assessment could be reviewed if appropriate guarantees were provided by the republic, applying for recognition, possibly by means of a referendum of all the citizens of the -- of BH, SRBH, without distinction, carried out under international supervision. Now, that, in a sense, I'd suggest to you, Mr. Treanor, that represented, if you like, good and bad news for the Bosnian Serbs, in this sense, that the -- if you like, the good was that it really vindicated their position, didn't it, that the steps taken by the SDA and the HDZ were steps beyond what ought properly to have been done because the will of the people, as the Serbs were saying, hadn't been fully determined and established?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I think I said in my testimony, yes, it was good news for the Bosnian Serbs, and I think I indicated something to the effect that obviously the steps that had been taken by the SDS leadership in establishing the Assembly and various resolutions and activities of the Assembly had -- which were among the materials considered by the commission, as indicated in its report, had had an effect on the commission and made it render this ruling, that the recognition cannot be granted immediately because it was apparent that there were very important segments in Bosnia that were opposed to independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bad news, and say if this is a wrong understanding of what is here, but the bad news is this, wasn't it, that talk of a referendum of all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina without distinction carried significant danger for the Serbs that actually that referendum would simply go in favour of independence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without entering into the interpretation of this sentence, which I think has been hotly contested ever since, I think that is broadly correct. I mean, we see that in fact what happened was that there was a referendum which -- in which anyone was permitted to vote, and it was supposed to be open to all. The Bosnian Serbs under the guidance of the SDS chose to boycott that, their position being that they had already had their referendum. Therefore, that significant portion of the population did not take part in the referendum. The referendum, of course, delivered a favourable vote among those that did vote, and about a month later, recognition was forthcoming. So yes, there was a danger lurking in there for them, for the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which, from your reading of the documentation, can you say that the danger was very well appreciated by the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the -- the discussion that I can recall relates to the -- the response to the -- holding the referendum and that sort of thing. I would say yes. I mean, they definitely appreciated that this was not necessarily a good thing for them, and they had a lot of discussion about how to handle it. Their attitude toward the referendum, on the one hand, and other steps that they may take to counter that, to continue to make it clear to the outside world that they continued to be opposed to recognition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it correct what they were involved in was a continuation of this very difficult political juggling act which was that there had been this commission set up by the European Community, so they, being involved in international negotiations, they would have wanted to be as receptive and cooperative as they could be with what was coming from this commission appointed by the EC, but, on the other hand, being aware of the lurking danger implicit in that conclusion, there was only so far they could ever go?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had choices before them as to what to do, and I think I set out in the documents that I presented the path that they followed, namely, as far as the referendum per se was concerned, once that decision was taken, which is another decision they opposed in the Assembly and that decision they hotly disputed the validity of that decision, taken in the end of January 1991 in the Bosnian Assembly about holding the referendum, then they had to consider their position toward that referendum. At the same time, they were pursuing international negotiations, and on another track they were proceeding with the establishment of their own governmental institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could then -- you could put aside, please -- and that's 7 you've got at the moment, isn't it. If you could put that aside and be given 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not currently, so far as I'm aware, receiving any gentle reprimands from the interpreters. I hope that means that no news is good news and that the pace is all right for them. I'm receiving a visual signal that confirms that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: For the record. I look forward to the visual signal where the position is opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They will know exactly how to stop you, Mr. Stewart, when necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we could take the first tab. That's 84 in bundle 8. And I think you highlighted a number of comments, but I certainly don't want to grind through them all, Mr. Treanor. But you highlight particularly at 18, 1-8, the middle of the page. This is the 26th of January. So this was fairly hot after the report of the Badinter Commission, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he -- Mr. Krajisnik says in the middle of page 18: In fact, the conclusion is that the Council of Ministers be tasked with drafting a decision on calling the referendum to be held 30 days following the completion of the transformation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which would be agreed by all three national communities, with a view to transforming Bosnia and Herzegovina into a composite, confederate community comprising of three legal identities." So this contained the -- what had really been a consistent element, hasn't it, in one form or another of the Bosnian Serb position, that got to be approval, some way or another, on behalf of all three of the nationalities, as a precondition to moving ahead with a change?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, broadly speaking. I mean, initially, the issue, back in the fall of 1991, was simply independence versus remaining in Yugoslavia for the whole of Bosnia. By this time, the Bosnian Serb leadership I think has become aware that their preferred option, that is that the whole of Bosnia stay in Yugoslavia, was not going to happen. And so they adopted a new strategy, namely, the transformation, which is the word used here, and that was the word that Dr. Karadzic liked to use, that Bosnia must be transformed internally, and then we can talk about the independence of Bosnia or whatever entities may be within the transformed Bosnia, but only after this transformation has taken place can we consider the issue of independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By this time, they were in this position, weren't they, that, following the Badinter Commission, as far as the European Community is concerned, there could be no independence of Bosnia without a referendum?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the Bosnian Serb leadership here, as we see, [indiscernible] as part of the jigsaw is no referendum without agreement among the three nationalities?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On transformation, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the transformation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By the way, just to remark that I think that among the items in dispute about that sentence in the Badinter Commission, one of them is whether the referendum really is a satisfactory condition for recognition or simply an example of one of the types of things that could be done. But certainly within Bosnia, it was taken to mean that, that: Okay, now we have to have a referendum and the referendum will decide the issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Presumably, that comment is based on -- the comment you've just made, Mr. Treanor, is based on the sentence in the report: This assessment -- the assessment that they hadn't fully established the will of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina could be reviewed if appropriate guarantees are provided by, in this case, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then it says possibly by means of a referendum of all the citizens. So that implies that, if it's possibly by that means could possibly be by some other means. That's what you're talking about, are you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is -- you said the transformation was a favourite word of -- well, you said Dr. Karadzic, and I think you probably meant Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, it's being used in this case by Mr. Krajisnik. This is what we're looking at at page 18?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic wouldn't have had a monopoly on words in Serbian. Is the transformation in English, is it in fact a close reflection of the Serbian word, in other words, implying, as I suggest it does, some neutrality as to what the changes might be?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a very interesting question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About that, anyway.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word is a long word in Serbian. It's from the Latin, so it's not a Serbian word. And I believe Dr. Karadzic indicated in discussions of this issue that this was a word they should use because basically what they were talking about was some sort of partition. But the international community would not accept partition. So they couldn't talk about partition. We'll talk about transformation, but that's in fact what it was, was a partition of the country into, as it's put here, three legal identities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say, Mr. Treanor, that, just looking at the remark that Mr. Krajisnik makes in the middle of page 18 of that document at tab 84, that he talks about the transformation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which would be agreed by all three national communities, with a view to transforming, using the word again, Bosnia and Herzegovina into a composite, confederate community, comprising three legal identities, that it wouldn't have been very difficult for anybody to read into that, "partition"? Wouldn't have been difficult to --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't have thought so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wouldn't have thought it was difficult?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And the position being adopted -- well, at this point, there's no -- there had been no suggestion of any difference between any views expressed by Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik at this point on this point?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any differences between them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were no differences between any views expressed by Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik on this issue at this time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I can recollect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that -- I know you're sometimes reluctant on such questions, Mr. Treanor, but that was a -- that was a politically realistic judgement for the Bosnian Serb leadership to have adopted at this time, wasn't it, in the context of the Badinter report and what had already happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which judgement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The judgement that transformation, in not very heavily coded terms, implying partition within Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was a politically realistic judgement for them to have adopted?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, realistic, and indeed, in the end, successful. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unhappily, yes. But also realistic in this sense, that it was -- it was, if you like, it was on the spectrum, it was somewhere in the area which at least held out some hope of quelling, dampening down the momentum towards some sort of civil war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I think they perceived it in that fashion and indeed that formed the basis of the negotiations that took place under international auspices after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if we go on to page -- same document, tab 84 in this bundle. If we go on to page 19.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same document, page 19?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you had drawn attention -- you had highlighted some further comments by Mr. Krajisnik on that page, that the -- he said: We have adopted -- do you see about 15 lines up I think it is from the bottom: We have adopted two conclusions.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a rather larger passage than the particular point you cited. We have adopted two conclusions after all. One of them was to declare null and void those decisions that were adopted at that illegal session. And that plainly refers back to October 14th, 15th, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The reference here, I believe, is to the assembly session of the 25th of January, at which the decision to hold a referendum was adopted in circumstances similar to the adoption of the platform and memorandum in October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I see. Thank you. And then second, the conclusion is that: We in fact tasked the Council of Ministers to draft a decision for the next session of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In it we will also express our readiness to go to the referendum once certain conditions are met. And those would be the same -- broadly the same conditions we were looking at a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it goes on then that the transformation, we see that word again, the transformation of Bosnia and Herzegovina be carried out 30 days thereafter. We can go to the referendum. As regards the nature of that decision, it's going to look like, however, let us leave it to the Council of Ministers to draft it and submit it at the next session. We will fix the date, as Mr. Vjestica said, we must sit in some sort of a permanent session. We must also meet the deadlines. And you cited in your evidence, this was at page 1561, you cited that very last bit and commented -- well, in fact, Mr. Tieger cited it and then you commented: Yes, so this is Mr. Krajisnik's agreement with the desire to complete the legislative programme necessary for establishing the state as soon as possible. This is an example, isn't it, very specifically and clearly, of Mr. Krajisnik doing his principal job as president of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a good example of him guiding the Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course -- well, a part of his job. Of course I say his prinicipal job. Of course he had to chair and guide the Assembly sessions, but also plan them and organise the timetables and then --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you say you suppose. That's obvious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's obvious, but again, I don't have documents that show that process, the pre-assembly process, what happened, how the agenda was set, this, that, and the other thing. All we have are the records of the assembly itself. I suppose something like that happened, though. But I can only suppose it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's a realistic inference from -- in fact, what the published constitutional and procedural responsibilities of the president were --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Rules of Procedure of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I had in mind the Rules of Procedure included in that, which I think you referred to those specifically in Article 26. It sets out the president's responsibilities and the fact that, well, they seemed to manage to meet, so from all that, we -- just an inference that Mr. Krajisnik was not recording it formally, but involved in setting all that up.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be my supposition, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then at page 21 of the same document, at the very bottom of the page, Mr. Krajisnik again -- the passage you've cited: Sir, let us be clear. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a conclusion of the Council of Ministers to draft for the next session of the Assembly of the Serbian People a decision on how to communicate a demand to the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the partition balance sheet. And you initially in your evidence - this is at page 1563 - you referred to this matter as a rather obscure one, but I think in fairness, you came to accept that it wasn't quite that obscure. You had suggested it was due to the annual budget, but in fact it's looking ahead, if you like, but it's looking to one -- I was going to say inevitable, but you don't like that word so much, Mr. Treanor. It was looking to one practical consequence of transformation, i.e., partition, which was that the country's assets would have to be split up, the country's finances would have to be reorganised.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was looking forward to that, as far as I can understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then not long after this, the -- of course, the international negotiations were going on, as you've confirmed, but not very long after this, in February, there was a session, negotiating session, in Lisbon, wasn't there, on 21st, 22nd of February?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move into the Lisbon session, how much time would it need? Because otherwise I'd like to have a break now for 20 minutes and then continue for another hour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No problem at all, Your Honour. Again, I'm entirely in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break until a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, we were just considering Lisbon and Lisbon agreement, 21st, 22nd of February. In a nutshell, the fundamental point of the Lisbon agreement, which was reached between the Bosnian Serbs, but also involved agreement of the Muslims under Mr. Izetbegovic's leadership, were these, weren't they, first of all, to preserve the existing external borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and secondly, to form national territorial units within Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that represented a -- maybe a positive one in this case, but a turnaround by Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's fair to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, if we -- if you could take document number 93, please. We're in bundle 8, tab 93. These are notes of the 8th Session of the Serb Assembly. So February 1991. I'm sorry, February 1992. Page 20. It's -- in this case, I can say it's page 23 of the B/C/S version. And Mr. Krajisnik is speaking - you referred to this at page 1600 of the transcript - as a participant in the Lisbon talks himself. And then he set out two options which you refer to there in the middle of the page one to fight by political means and then to break off talks and go to force. At the foot of this same page, Mr. Krajisnik says: And the taboo of indivisibility, wholeness, non-division was thus removed. We consider this a 30 to 40 per cent success, but it's still a long way to go from the ultimate success. That's why Mr. Koljevic's suggestion is good to sort all this out today to be aware of what it is that our representatives advocate. And he says: I absolutely refuse the discussion on whether you have or do not have confidence in me. Anyone more suitable should take his place in the talks and negotiations immediately without any discussion, irrespective of Messrs. Koljevic and Karadzic only the best players may play this game. Sometimes a game is better played by the players from the bench than by the first team and no apologies should be made here. Now, I suggest to you, Mr. Treanor, that this is interesting because this is Mr. Krajisnik classifying himself as somebody coming off the bench for these purposes rather than being a member of the first team, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me look at the original. Well, what I get out of this, quite frankly, is something that I think I first studied in Latin class back in --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometime ago?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we call junior high school in the United States, the seventh or eighth grade, Cicero or somebody, the rhetorical device of saying, oh, I'm not so good, so please replace me, and then it was oh, no, no, no, we need you. This is, in my view, a rhetorical device, the whole passage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, that may be so up to a point, mightn't it, but I don't want to get too Ciceronian about it, but even as a rhetorical device, would you agree, unless it's got some element of truth in it for the audience, it's not going to work, is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends what the element of truth is. The element of truth, in order to make it work, is that the audience, in this case the assemblies, want him to be on the team. You're focusing in on this that the best players and the players from the bench. I mean, I can hardly believe from what I've read that the members of the Assembly would consider Mr. Krajisnik not to be among the best players.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to get into too much of an academic debate, and I'm trying to think of an analogy, but if Pele had said to the population of Brazil, sometimes you don't need your first team players and people have to come off the bench, so here I am, would have been just -- you're talking -- maybe Pele doesn't mean a thing to you, Mr. Treanor. But if he was absolutely blindingly obviously a first team player, it would have been a silly remark to make and it wouldn't have had any effect, as he wished it to have on the audience. There's got to be some truth in the fact that he is not in the same category and league for these purposes as Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic, for the rhetorical device to have any chance of working; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just not obvious to me. In fact, the reference could be, and again, this is probably a rather off-the-cuff remark, but the reference could be to the idea: Don't be hesitant to put in someone who is not as important as I am into this, because maybe they're better than I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you an additional question? Because I had some difficulties in understanding what -- to whom he was referring when he said sometimes a game is better played by the players from the bench than by the first team. Was he referring to the players on the bench as those who would possibly replace him, or would he refer to the players of the bench as himself, as is suggested in the question by Mr. Stewart? Is there anything in the original language that would favour the one or the other interpretation of this sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't think so, Your Honour. I'll look at it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I was puzzled who was on the bench and who was on the first team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can actually offer Mr. Treanor the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I didn't realise he had got it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a problem. No, I don't think the original is different here. I don't think it helps. The translation is adequate. But, as I say, I think that the sense may be that he's referring to his potential replacement as being someone from the bench. If you think someone is better than I am --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can simply invite you to -- it's only say a couple of sentences. Could you -- because you're homing in on it as opposed to doing the whole document. Could you offer us your translation of -- I think that paragraph, three or four sentences: I absolutely refuse. That's the translation we've got at the moment.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I will in no way discuss about that." I'm doing it kind of literally here because of the word order. Whether I have or don't have confidence. Right away, without discussion, whoever is more suitable must take a place, accomplish, perform, the discussions and negotiations, independently of Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic. Here the best players, quote unquote, must play in this quote unquote match. Sometimes those who are in reserve as players know how to play the match better than the first ones and there is no pardon here, no excuse, no need for -- there's no pardon here, literally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may ultimately have been a matter of reading and argument, but I do suggest to you that on any translation and reading, it's clear what he's saying is: The best players, in other words, the best people must go into these negotiations. Sometimes the best people for a particular purpose or a particular game, particular negotiation, are not the first team players but the reserves or those coming off the bench, and I'm making no apology, because in that case that's me. I'm one of the best people for this particular negotiation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the witness has answered the question that he interpreted these lines in a different way, that he -- the persons to enter the team would be the ones on the bench, not Mr. Krajisnik. That's how I understood your interpretation. And now you repeat the same issue. If I'm wrong, Mr. Treanor, please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, what I was doing, was as one sometimes needs to do, is, having given the witness the opportunity of doing his own translation and looking at it again, I was giving him the opportunity of reconsidering his answer. Now, it may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The result --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You repeated your own position in interpreting what it meant. In reading the original language and giving your translation, does this change your mind or on your first interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, very shortly afterwards, by -- in fact, before the end of February, Mr. Izetbegovic drew back, didn't he, very clearly, from his agreement of the Lisbon document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we then go on, please, to 9, bundle or file 9. Go to tab 96, please. Now, this is a decision on proclaiming the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was published in the Official Gazette. And then you highlighted a number of matters. In Article 1, which is at page -- well, it's at page 2. It's not difficult to find Article 1. It comes very early in the document. Sorry. I had forgotten a few minutes ago that you are operating consistently with the B/C/S versions of these documents this morning, or this afternoon, Mr. Treanor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've been looking at the translations since that's what you're giving the references to. I haven't discovered or noticed any particular translation problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just wasn't clear. I got the impression a few minutes ago, and a member of my team informed me you were operating from the B/C/S files or bundles. But it's the English one you've got in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, they're both here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've got both. No problem. Right. Article 1, the Republic -- this was your evidence, 1629 of the transcript: The Republic is defined as the state of the Serbian people and of the citizens living in it. And you commented that the word "all" which we see here wasn't in the original. In fact, it's the obvious sense, anyway, isn't it, even without the word "all," the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the state of the Serb people and the citizens living therein. It's not going to be different, is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's an interesting question. There are no articles in Serbian as there are in English. So whereas in English the word -- coupling the word "all" with "the" in this context may seem redundant. In Serbian, to my knowledge, it is not, since there is no article in Serbian. So it says: Of citizens living in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we've covered Cicero between us this morning, Mr. Treanor, so I don't want to get into too much refined detail about the Serbian language. But you'd add the "and" anyway, wouldn't you, so it would be the state of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the state of Serb people and citizens living therein?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be a literal translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Anyway, perhaps it's not valuable to pursue this, although it wasn't in the original, that's what we have here. And then you say this in contrast to a similar provision in the BH constitution which mentioned three peoples. So you say -- what you said in your evidence early, so this state, as the article defines it, is a state of only one people. And then you say: Therefore, I think it's safe to say that under this article, only one people is being given rights as a people. Now, that -- I suggest to you, Mr. Treanor, of course you've got the advantage of the Serbian version -- well, actually, what you really have the advantage of is understanding Serbian. But I suggest to you it's not saying that. It may be giving some primacy, in an obvious sense, to the Serb people, but it is not, even if we just look at Article 1 on its own, it is not defining this as a state of only one people, is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The article says what it says. We've been over that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it doesn't say what --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was calling the Court's attention to the fact that this differs from the wording in, for instance, the Bosnian constitution, in which three peoples were mentioned. The whole basis of practically every document that I've presented in the course of my testimony is that that constitution gave the Serbian people, as a people, certain rights within Bosnia and Herzegovina, rights which the SDS were determined to see defended. So they attached very important -- very high significance to the wording of the corresponding article in the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The fact that the wording here is different is therefore not simply inevitable, as you might put it, but is purposeful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, it wouldn't be the Defence case that there's anything different. After all, it would be -- it would be naive to the point of ridiculous to suggest that drafters of the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the circumstances in which it was created, are not going to reflect some special position of Serbs. That's what it's all about. All I'm trying to do at the moment is to seek your agreement that what you said in your evidence earlier is actually inaccurate and exaggerated, that this article does not define this state as a state of only one people, because, apart from everything else, it defines it as a state of the Serb people and all the citizens living therein, whoever they might be.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, the corresponding article in the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina contained similar wording. It mentioned other citizens. Despite that, and I'm not challenging the interpretation, the interpretation of the leadership of the SDS of the mention of the Serbian people along with the other peoples conferred certain rights on the Serbian people - I think I'm repeating - within that entity which had to be exercised by the Serbian people as such. Their rights could not be subsumed into -- and I realise I'm getting into areas of constitutional law that perhaps are beyond me, but I'm merely trying to repeat their arguments, as we've seen them in the documents -- could not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be subsumed among the mass of the citizenry, for instance, in a referendum of all the citizens. So for them, having the particular peoples enumerated is very important. Now, as you say, it's rather logical that they're going to enumerate the Serbs, since this is a Serbian entity. But that ipso facto, in their line of reasoning, deprives other national communities of the types of rights within their republic that they sought to exercise within the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at Article 5, same page. Not hard to find. The constitutional order of the Republic is based on the following: Guarantee and protection of human freedoms and rights in compliance with international standards. And then assurance of national equality. Then social justice, reign of justice, which may be rule of law, probably, as an alternative translation. And then free elections and so on. And the last one, protection of rights of ethnic groups and other minorities. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 7, official language, Serbian language. But Mr. Treanor, you gave evidence about the meaning of these articles in your earlier evidence. It's not unusual or sinister to find an official language declared in a written constitution, is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 7?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first limb, declaring Serbian as the official language. I'm saying -- suggesting to you that's not -- it's not an unusual provision to find in a modern democratic state's constitution.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that it's unusual. And I'm not sure what my original testimony on this point was. However, the name of the language was an issue that was rather vigorously debated. And when I say that, I mean not between, necessarily - I haven't seen that. There may be such discussion - between the SDS and the other coalition partners, but within the Bosnian Serb Assembly they had quite a little debate on the language law in later months. And there were rather sharp differences of opinion as to what the name of the language should be. So that is in issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a slightly different point, but I think perhaps I'll move on. The second limb of Article 7, having stated Serbian as the official language and the -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I may. It appears to me that Mr. Treanor is being challenged on the attention he drew to Article 7 in his examination-in-chief, at least that's part of the premise of the questioning. As I examine the transcript, I don't believe that Mr. Treanor did draw attention to Article 7, and I'm certainly not objecting to any questions about it, but I think that premise should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could you give us the page where Mr. -- unless there's any -- you couldn't clarify or you think it would not be proper to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The -- Your Honour, the position is this: I don't believe I did suggest that Mr. Treanor had referred to Article 7 in his evidence earlier, because I don't believe he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then at least you agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure where it leads us, Your Honour, but I think I can agree on that. I stand corrected, as always, by the transcript if I did, but I don't believe I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think you said that. You said: First limb declaring Serbian as the official language. I'm suggesting to you that it's not -- it's not an unusual provision to find in a modern democratic state's constitution. And the second limb --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't wish to draw into attention, but I think the reference I was referring to occurred just prior to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you do agree, we had better not pursue the matter and proceed. And I'll look at the transcript anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the position is very simple. Mr. Treanor did refer to Article 1, to Article 2, to Article 3, to Article 5 expressly in his evidence. I don't believe he did refer to Article 7, but on the other hand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You agree on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- anyway, where were we? In regions -- we were in regions inhabited by groups speaking other languages. The language and script shall also be used in the manner as provided by the law. Well, it's got as provided by the law. But it's clear the thrust of this is it's the linguistic aspect of general protection of minority rights, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Article 10, which I believe is another one you didn't refer to in your earlier evidence, Article 10 states that citizens of the Republic have equal rights in their freedom, rights and obligations, they're equal before the law and enjoy the same legal protection regardless of race, sex, language, ethnic origin, religion, social background, birth, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. That, well, I hesitate to say, couldn't be clearer. It is very clear, isn't it, as a specific statement that everybody, every citizen, is equal before the law?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's pretty standard stuff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be pretty standard stuff, Mr. Treanor, but it's standard stuff because well-drafted constitutions require it and should have it, and it's a proper reflection of those international standards in recognised democracies?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And standard stuff in this sense, that if enforced, you're safe as a citizen, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If enforced, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With mild hesitation, in the light of the question a few minutes ago, but I'm inviting you to reconsider your simple description of Article 1, when, after all, it's looked at in the context of all those other provisions as providing that this state is a state of only one people. Is that --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, without getting too far into legal and theory interpretation, the issue that is posed by Article 1 and the comparable article in the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I don't think that issue is not covered here. The issue is whether, as the Serb posed it, in my understanding, the way the SDS leadership posed this issue, was whether a constituent people, in this case -- in their case, the Serbian people, had the right to prevent the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia. That was the first issue. I don't -- then the comparable issue here would be: Does anyone have the right to take part of this Serbian Republic that we're forming out of the Republic? I don't think those issues are addressed in those articles. And I'm speaking off the top of my head, since you posed the question, and I don't want to get -- I can't get too far into legal reasoning and interpretation. But the force of the article and the constitution of the Socialist Republic dealt with matters that, as far as I can understand, are not covered in these other articles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, I think -- well, I don't think. I know, because I can read it. In your earlier evidence, it's at page 1629 of the transcript, you did refer specifically to Article 3 and the statement in Article 3 that the Republic is part of the Federal State of Yugoslavia. And then you pointed out, absolutely correctly, that there is no reference here, for instance, to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, first of all, the -- a difficulty, if you like, with the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina being part of the Federal State of Yugoslavia was, if you like, at the Federal State of Yugoslavia end. I think you gave evidence to the effect that the federal -- Belgrade was saying: Well, actually, we can't do that. We can't offer you that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a certain point in time that seems to have been communicated to them, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the fact that there was no reference to Bosnia and Herzegovina, was that not in a sense the -- forget that, Mr. Treanor. I won't press the next question. The -- yes. You drew attention, as I said, to the fact that there was no reference to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The literal words are there, of course, but they're only there as part of the definition of the Serb Republic. That the -- it was a combination, whatever the attitude of Belgrade, the combination of the Serb -- Bosnian Serb leadership's wish and clear stated wish to remain part of the Federal State of Yugoslavia, if -- I use Belgrade to try and make it clear, if Belgrade would have them, put together with the Bosnian Muslim position of declaration of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, inevitably - inevitably - logically led to there being no reference in this constitution to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you made reference to a declaration of independence. There really wasn't a declaration of independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll perhaps rephrase that. Policy of independence. Rather long question. Perhaps I'll --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm fine. Again, there's nothing inevitable about any of this. In fact, there was quite a bit of discussion in the Assembly about these articles and whether there should or should not be a reference to being part of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or not. I can't recall precisely, but that may even have been in the initial draft that was presented to the Assembly. But certainly, as you indicated, it's obviously an issue, and in that connection, I would point out again -- let's look at the date of this document. It's the 28th of February, before the referendum was taking place and way before the recognition of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina took place. So, in my layman's understanding of -- I guess it's international law, the people who were doing this were still within the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But this is -- that was a fact which they ultimately chose not to include in this document, obviously reflecting their intention not to be part of that state should it become independent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the -- so you said there was debate. The alternative -- well, obviously, the alternative to not mentioning Bosnia and Herzegovina is to mention it. If it had been expressly mentioned, then it would presumably, then, Mr. Treanor, have been mentioned, if it was worth mentioning at all, in terms which recognised that the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was within the -- within --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was apparently the thrust. And of course that was the object or the stated object of the negotiations that were under way, that this new Bosnia-Herzegovina, whatever it was going to be called, would be composed of three entities. This was one of the entities and they would all be within the new Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think one of the reasons -- I can only speculate on that. But they left that out. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Bosnia and Herzegovina became independent, and I'm talking about Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole, if Bosnia and Herzegovina became independent, then clearly Article 3 of this constitution would have to go, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as it stands now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as it stands now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to this text, this entity is part of Yugoslavia. It doesn't make any reference to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The only reference is in Article 4, that they can make agreements with other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So if Bosnia and Herzegovina becomes independent, and I think that's what I was going to say before, that would not necessitate a change in this constitution, and I think that may be one of the reasons why they decided to leave it out, to leave their options open, so to speak, and not have to amend the constitution contingent on the results of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm not making myself clear, Mr. Treanor. The -- if this constitution had expressly stated that the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, right, and if Bosnia and Herzegovina became independent, an independent state, okay, so that's one and two, it would have been inconsistent, then, for the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to continue to say, as is stated in Article 3 here, that the Republic is a part of the Federal State of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, yes. And what I'm suggesting is what they would have done is to amend the part that says that they are part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what it comes down to, then, really, is this, does it, and this is a question, Mr. Treanor, after all: That, in effect, this constitution, as drafted, was already adapted as drafted to, in its effect, to independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It took that contingency into account. Perhaps the confusion arises over the -- something to do with the attitude of the Bosnian Serb leadership at this time. Their attitude at this time was that if the non-Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina want to leave Yugoslavia, that's fine with us, but we're staying in. So, I mean, that was a decision that -- a standpoint that they had adopted some time ago, and I thought I was trying to indicate is reflected in this constitution. This is saying that our entity is staying in Yugoslavia. The rest of you can do what you want.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's entirely consistent with that. And that clearly, then, would be -- well, if you like, socially and culturally, it clearly would be then the new Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it clearly would be predominantly a Serb society, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under which contingency?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Bosnian Muslims and the Croats, for that matter, they leave federal Yugoslavia, and the Bosnian Serbs stay within it.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would depend on the borders of the Serbian entity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, any borders which made any sense of the exercise at all would have the effect that the new Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be predominantly and clearly a basically Serb society?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if by Serb you mean having a predominantly Serbian population, I don't think that's the case. Any borders which made any sense of the exercise at all. Well, whose sense? As we've seen in the documents that I presented, the Bosnian Serb leaders consistently and repeatedly claimed 65 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
